sentences.text: The genus Unquillosaurus contains only one species, U. ceibalii, known solely from a single fossilized pubis bone — the pelvic bone that supports the hind leg.
Based on this fragment, scientists estimate the animal reached 3 meters in length, stood 1.40 meters high, and weighed nearly 40 kilograms.
The holotype specimen PVL 3670-11 was discovered at Arroyo-Morterito in the Los Blanquitos Formation and was formally described by Jaime Eduardo Powell in 1979.
Powell originally assigned Unquillosaurus to the Carnosauria in 1979, a group of large carnivorous dinosaurs.
However, in 2004, Novas and Agnolin concluded that the animal belonged to Maniraptora or at least Maniraptoriformes based on its opisthopubic pelvic anatomy.
Later, Martínez and Novas suggested in 2006 that Unquillosaurus likely belonged to the maniraptoran clade Dromaeosauridae.
In 2012, Carrano and colleagues classified it as a member of Carcharodontosauridae due to similarities with Giganotosaurus.
By 2024, researchers considering the taxonomy of Diuqin suggested Unquillosaurus might be a member of the Unenlagiinae.
Currently, the Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Unquillosaurus as Carcharodontosauridae.
Unquillosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 83 to 71 million years ago in the Campanian stage in what is now South America.

Initially, Unquillosaurus was thought to belong to a giant theropod 11 meters long, but in 2012, Carrano et al. reclassified the animal into Carnosauria, specifically Carcharodontosauria, suggesting the original interpretation was likely correct.
